name: Purple Grey
lede: Purple grey is a descriptive name for a dull violet that has almost lost its hue, a color the books touch only in passing.

sections.title: Two old opinions
sections.body:
Birren held in 1950 that purple, a blend of red and blue, is more or less neutral biologically, a poor choice for broad surfaces because it upsets the eye's focus, and the hue with the most purely aesthetic appeal [1]. That is old opinion rather than modern evidence, and the classification of purple as neutral in this sense has not been confirmed by later books.

A text on color manners quoted by Pastoureau advised older women against white, the color of youth, and toward tan, purple, gray or black [2]. Grey and purple appear there as sober colors, not as one color.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 21 works [3]. Two early examples are Frederik Rohde's *Vinterlandskab* of 1848 and J. L. Camradt's *Blomster i en skål* of 1830, both Danish [3]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].

notes.cite: Birren, Color Psychology and Color Therapy, ch. 20 ("The Prescription of Color")
Pastoureau, White: The History of a Color, p. 115
